family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Start at the inflorescence, but do not demand a classic compound umbel. Then confirm an inferior 2-carpellate ovary, usually sheathing leaf bases, and a dry schizocarp that separates into two mericarps.
core_characters: Leaves usually alternate, often compound or deeply lobed; petiole base commonly expanded into a sheath.
Inflorescences commonly simple or compound umbels, but some lineages such as Eryngium compress flowers into dense heads.
Two styles often arise from a swollen stylopodium/nectar disk.
Fruit is typically a dry schizocarp splitting into 2 one-seeded mericarps.
Mericarps often bear ribs and oil canals (vittae), which can be important in technical identification.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not define Apiaceae as 'white umbrella flowers.' Eryngium is a local counterexample.
Do not call every umbel-bearing plant Apiaceae; inspect ovary position and fruit.
Do not confuse a schizocarp with a capsule.

Asteraceae.confusion: Dense heads can make Eryngium look thistle-like or composite-like.
Asteraceae.tie_breaker: Apiaceae flowers retain the inferior bicarpellate ovary and split into two mericarps; Asteraceae has a capitulum of florets with an involucre and cypsela/pappus system.

Araliaceae.confusion: Related family with umbels and inferior ovaries.
Araliaceae.tie_breaker: Apiaceae is mostly herbaceous and has a dry 2-merous schizocarp; Araliaceae is more often woody with fleshy drupe-like fruits.

cards.look_here_first: Look at the flower cluster as a whole: it is a dense elongated head/spike wrapped in stiff spiny bracts, not a thistle and not a classic carrot-family umbel.
confirm: Annual, usually single-stemmed below the branched flowering canopy.
Leaves become deeply lobed and strongly spinose upward; many cauline leaves sheath the stem substantially at the node.
Inflorescences are dense headlike spikes with an involucre of spreading spiny bracts.
Individual flowers are tiny, 5-merous and sit on an inferior ovary.
Fruit belongs to the Apiaceae schizocarp/mericarp system; do not label it a true capsule.
cards.teaching_value: Excellent exception card demonstrating why family ID must use ovary/fruit/leaf-base characters, not inflorescence gestalt alone.
cards.source_disagreement_note: Some horticultural/native-plant summaries casually call the fruit a capsule. For the canonical family lesson, use the authoritative Apiaceae morphology: dry schizocarp dividing into two mericarps.
